sentences.text: Alder had 13 readmissions among its 30 patients. Is that a lot?
In Episode 3 we got two answers. Against everyone pooled together, 1.4 times what was expected. Against everyone but Alder itself, 1.8.
So we asked for two things: a risk rule learned from patients who share a clinic, and a yardstick no single clinic can bend.
The risk rule arrived with the dial. Today, the yardstick.
Here is the idea. Keep Alder's 30 patients exactly as they are, and send them, on paper, to the middle clinic.
Would they have more than 13 readmissions there, or fewer?
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: swap the curve.
First, the yardstick. Line up the five sliders, and take the one in the middle.
It is Cedar's, at minus 1.52. And as we saw last time, it stays put wherever Elm's slider happens to stop.
Draw that clinic's curve in grey, and call it the reference.
At the reference, a lower-risk patient has an 18% chance of readmission. A higher-risk patient, 62%.
Notice what kind of thing the reference is. Not an average patient. A clinic: one clinic's level, applied to whoever walks in.
Here are Alder's patients on Alder's own curve: 24 lower-risk patients at 34%, and 6 higher-risk at 80%.
Add up those chances, and you get 13. Exactly what Alder observed, because the fit balanced it.
Now swap the curve. The same 30 patients, on the grey one: 24 at 18%, and 6 at 62%.
Add those up: 8.02.
So at the reference, these same patients would expect about 8 readmissions. At Alder, there were 13.
13 over 8.02 is 1.62. Alder had 62% more readmissions than its own patients would be expected to have at the reference clinic.
That is the whole method. Keep the patients. Swap the curve. Count.
Do the same for every clinic. Alder, 1.62. Birch, 0.88. Cedar, exactly 1. Dune, 1.46. And Elm, zero.
Cedar comes out at exactly 1, because it is the reference, measured against itself.
So Alder's answer is neither 1.4 nor 1.8. It is 1.62.
And this yardstick is hard to bend. Push any one slider as far as you like, and the middle value moves no further than the next clinic along.
One thing has changed since Episode 3. Against the pooled standard, the expected counts added up to the 42 observed. Against the middle clinic, they add up to 38.8.
The clinics no longer break even as a group, and they need not.
Ratios are often reported as rates. Multiply each one by the overall readmission rate, 41%.
Alder becomes 66%. Birch, 36. Cedar, 41. Dune, 59. Elm, zero.
Read these with care. No patient at Alder had a 66% chance of readmission. It is the same ratio, moved to a more familiar scale.
One more connection. Move Alder's slider, and its ratio traces a single rising curve.
With the slider at the reference, the ratio is 1. At Alder's own gamma, 1.62.
So every statement about a gamma becomes a statement about a ratio. Episode 9's interval for Alder's gamma becomes an interval for its ratio: from 1.02 to 2.31.
Two cautions. First, a ratio of 1 means like the reference clinic. It does not mean good.
Second, always say which reference. Last time we tried a size-weighted average instead of the middle clinic. Against that, Alder's 1.62 becomes 1.87.
In our crowd of 200 providers, the ratios run from 0.44 to 1.99, with half on each side of 1.
Which of those are real differences, and which are luck? That question is coming.
Let's gather it up.
The reference is the middle clinic's curve.
Keep a clinic's patients, swap in that curve, and count: observed over expected.
And name the reference with every ratio.
We kept the patients and swapped the curve. Next time, the other way round: keep the curve, and swap the patients.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
